newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac, Kohl meet again on European reform.
newsitem.headline: Chirac, Kohl meet again on European reform.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met for the second time in four days on Tuesday to hammer out joint positions on the road to a single European currency and reform of the European Union.

Kohl arrived for the talks, set for nearly three hours and followed by a press statement, after EU finance ministers failed to agree on Monday night on a stability pact to impose budget discipline on members of the future European currency.

One diplomat said Paris and Bonn were in agreement on the issue and Germany, which has been isolated in seeking strict limits on budget deficits with automatic fines for violations except in numerically defined exceptional circumstances, would eventually settle for a less precise formula.

When they dined together in the French town of Perigueux on Saturday, Chirac and Kohl sought to calm currency market jitters caused by ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing's call for a depreciation of the franc to promote economic growth and jobs.
Chirac reaffirmed France's commitment to a stable parity between the franc and the deutschemark in the run up to economic and monetary union in 1999.

The financial markets apparently believed the message. The franc, boosted by a stronger dollar and a weaker mark due to slow German growth, has since regained nearly two centimes to trade at around 3.38 to the mark on Tuesday afternoon.

Diplomats said that in exchange for Chirac's support on the stability pact, Kohl was keen to accommodate French demands for greater coordination of European economic policies to boost growth and combat unemployment.
They said a compromise could involve increasing the powers and frequency of meetings of the ECOFIN Council and possibly having an annual economic summit.

Under fire from Eurosceptics in his own centre-right coalition, French Prime Minister Alain Juppe assured parliament last week that political authorities, not just the independent European central bank, would set the EU's economic policy and the euro's exchange rate after monetary union.

France's insistence on a strong role for government economic policy has been at variance with Germany's emphasis, to reassure its own sceptical public opinion, that the independent central bank will guarantee the euro is as strong as the mark.

On European Union reform, diplomats said Chirac and Kohl would put the finishing touches to a joint letter to the other 13 EU leaders proposing treaty changes to be discussed at their December 13-14 Dublin summit.

A senior French official said the proposals mainly covered building a common foreign and defence policy and harmonising EU policies on interior and justice affairs such as immigration, asylum, visas, drugs, organised crime and terrorism.
He said the letter would contain no precise suggestions on the most difficult issue of changing the weighted voting system for EU decisions or reducing the size of the European Commission.
Nor would it deal with the powers of the European Parliament and of national parliaments, on which Paris and Bonn have yet to reach agreement, he said.
